listeningScripts.title: Hiring a Coach for a Group Trip
listeningScripts.text:
Agent: Good afternoon, Dalebrook Coaches.
Caller: Hello, I'm organising a day trip for our walking group and I need to hire a coach.
Agent: Certainly. Can I take your name?
Caller: It's Winifred Aldersley. Aldersley is A-L-D-E-R-S-L-E-Y.
Agent: And a contact number?
Caller: 07351 664 209.
Agent: How many passengers?
Caller: Thirty-eight, possibly forty.
Agent: Then I'd put you on the fifty-three seater rather than the smaller one. The forty-nine seater would fit you, but with walking boots and packs you want the luggage space underneath, and the smaller coach doesn't have it.
Caller: That makes sense. What's the destination?
Agent: Where are you going?
Caller: Cairnhead, in the north of the county. About sixty miles.
Agent: And the date?
Caller: Sunday the eighteenth of May.
Agent: That's available. Pick-up time?
Caller: Eight in the morning, from the library on Market Street.
Agent: Fine. And return?
Caller: We'd want to leave Cairnhead about five.
Agent: The cost for that distance and duration is four hundred and twenty pounds. That includes the driver's hours; if you overrun by more than thirty minutes there's an additional charge, because the driver's day is limited by law rather than by us.
Caller: Understood. Is there a deposit?
Agent: A hundred pounds to hold the date, and the balance seven days before.
Caller: What about cancellation?
Agent: Full refund up to fourteen days before, half after that, nothing within forty-eight hours.
Caller: Sensible. Anything I should tell the group?
Agent: Two things. No hot food on board, and boots off or bagged if they're muddy — the driver cleans the coach himself between jobs. And give me a named contact who'll travel with the group, in case we need to reach somebody on the day.
Caller: That'll be me.
Agent: Perfect. I'll email the confirmation this afternoon.

listeningScripts.title: Exhibitor Briefing
listeningScripts.text:
Coordinator: Good morning, exhibitors, and welcome to the Fenwick Conference Centre. I'm Douglas, the events coordinator, and this briefing covers set-up and the rules of the building.

Timings first. Set-up is tomorrow between six in the morning and eleven, and the hall opens to delegates at midday. I would encourage you to arrive early rather than at ten — the goods lift takes one stand at a time and the queue at half past nine is routinely forty minutes.

Stand rules. Nothing may be fixed to the walls, floors or pillars, and nothing may project beyond your allocated boundary, including banners that swing. The boundary matters more than people expect: an exhibitor overhanging by half a metre takes that space from the stand behind, and we do enforce it.

Electricity must be ordered in advance — we cannot supply it on the day. Every appliance you bring needs to have been tested and labelled, and we do check, because our insurance depends on it rather than on trust.

Now the building. Coming in through the main entrance, registration is directly ahead of you. The exhibition hall is on the left, through the wide doors, occupying the whole western side. The auditorium, used for the plenary sessions, is on the right of registration at the eastern end. The catering area is at the back of the exhibition hall, deliberately, so that delegates walk past the stands to reach the coffee. Breakout rooms are upstairs, above the auditorium, and the goods entrance — which is where you unload, not the main entrance — is at the rear of the building on the northern side.

One final point that is easy to forget. Take your rubbish and your packaging with you at the end. Waste left on a stand is charged for by weight, and the charge is genuinely large, because disposing of a hall's worth of packaging is a contract we have to pay for whether or not we recover it from anybody.

listeningScripts.title: Preparing for a Viva
listeningScripts.text:
Supervisor: So — your viva is in three weeks. How are you feeling about it?
Nour: Anxious. I keep re-reading the thesis.
Supervisor: That is the least useful preparation available, and almost everyone does it. You wrote it; you know what is in it. What you have not practised is talking about it.
Nour: What should I do instead?
Supervisor: Answer questions out loud, to a person. Ask a friend from another discipline to make you explain the whole thing in five minutes, then in one. If you cannot do it in one, you do not yet know what your argument is.
Nour: What will they actually ask?
Supervisor: The opening question is almost always some version of "summarise your contribution" or "why did you do this". Prepare that one properly — it is the only question you can be certain of, and a hesitant answer sets a tone that takes half an hour to recover.
Nour: And the hard ones?
Supervisor: They will find the weakest part of your method, because it is their job. The mistake is defending it as though it were strong. Say what the limitation is, say why you chose it given the constraints, and say what you would do differently. Examiners are testing whether you understand your own work, not whether it is flawless.
Nour: What if I don't know an answer?
Supervisor: Say so, and then think aloud about how you would find out. Silence is bad and invention is much worse — an examiner who catches you guessing will test everything else you have said.
Nour: Should I bring a copy of the thesis?
Supervisor: Yes, tabbed, with your own notes in it. Nobody is impressed by memory, and looking something up calmly reads as competence rather than weakness.
Nour: How long will it take?
Supervisor: Between two and three hours, usually. Eat beforehand — I have seen more vivas damaged by low blood sugar than by weak research.

listeningScripts.title: Why Screening Is Hard
listeningScripts.text:
Lecturer: Screening a healthy population for a disease sounds unambiguously good, and today I want to explain why it is one of the hardest interventions in medicine to get right.

Begin with what screening is. You take people with no symptoms and test them, hoping to find disease early enough to treat it better. The appeal is obvious and the intuition — that finding disease earlier must be better — is where the difficulty starts, because it is not always true.

The first problem is false positives. In a population where the disease is rare, even a very accurate test produces more false alarms than real detections, simply because there are so many more healthy people to be wrong about. Those people undergo further investigation, some of it invasive, with its own risks, and a proportion suffer lasting anxiety. Nothing has been found and harm has occurred.

The second problem is subtler and more important. Screening detects disease that would never have caused symptoms — growths that grow too slowly to matter within a lifetime, or that stop, or regress. Treating those people cannot help them, because they were never going to be harmed, and treatment carries real risk. This is called overdiagnosis, and it is invisible in the outcome data, because a person overdiagnosed and treated is recorded as a life saved.

That invisibility corrupts the obvious measure. Survival rates after diagnosis always improve when screening is introduced, partly because the clock starts earlier and partly because harmless cases enter the numbers. The only measure that cannot be fooled by either effect is whether deaths from the disease fall in the whole population, and that requires large trials over long periods.

Where those trials have been done, the results vary by disease rather than supporting a general answer. Some programmes clearly reduce mortality; some produce a small reduction with substantial overdiagnosis; and some have been withdrawn after showing no mortality benefit at all.

The conclusion I want you to take is not that screening is bad. It is that "we should test everybody" is a claim requiring evidence about that disease, that test and that population, and that the intuition it rests on — earlier is better — is exactly the thing being tested rather than a reason to skip the test.
